Business.title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate spying claims; UK chancellor ‘dismayed’ by budget leak – as it happened
Business.text:
Introduction: Nvidia, down $430bn, hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.

The crisis gripping Nvidia is gathering pace, with around $430bn wiped off the value of the world’s most valuable company since it was hit by a spying scandal.

Overnight, Nvidia announced it has hired a former top federal prosecutor to help probe chief executive Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company’s board have retained Joon H. Kim, the former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York, and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct “a thorough and independent investigation”.

Wachtell is a heavyweight corporate law firm. In 2022 it was hired by Twitter to force Elon Musk to complete his $44bn takeover, for example, and has a track record of advising major companies on issues such as mergers and corporate governance.

It will now look into the circumstances of Huang’s affair – thought to be with Alice Huang, who US officials believe is a Chinese spy, and who worked for Nvidia customer Megaspeed.

Although Beijing has denied allegations that it operated an espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s value has been buffeted this week.

Yesterday, its shares fell by almost 5.5%, adding to the 4.27% drop on Monday. This has pulled the company’s value down to $4.07tn, from $4.50tn before the story broke last weekend.

9.45am BST: ECB President Lagarde taking part on panel discussion at 9th Paris Peace Forum in Paris

Noon BST: US weekly mortgage approvals data

2.15pm GMT: Chancellor John Healey quizzed by Treasury committee on the budget

Updated at 03.35 EST

London stock market closes higher

And finally, the UK stock market has ended the day up almost 0.8%, on a decent day for shares.

The FTSE 100 share index has closed 84 points higher at 10,835, rising towards its record high.

Computer services company Computacenter (+4.7%) were the top riser, followed by investment group Polar Capital (+4%).

Congress 'set to subpoena Nvidia’s Jensen Huang'

Congress is prepared to subpoena Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to provide answers about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, a key House Republican said today.

Republican Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs a House China committee, said Huang has until the end of the day on Wednesday to respond to an earlier request to appear for a closed-door briefing about the scandal that has engulfed one of the world’s most valuable companies and its billionaire leader, Bloomberg reports.

If Huang does not agree to the briefing or suggest an alternative date, there will likely be subpoenas for him to appear, Moolenaar said in an appearance Wednesday on Fox Business.

Nvidia is holding its early stock market gains – up 3.8% to $175.34 in morning trading.

That narrows the market cap loss since Friday, before CEO Jensen Huang admitted to marital infidelity, to $272bn.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang tried to project “business as usual” as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC.

The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company’s quarterly earnings on November 17.

Ending the conflict in the Middle East would be the single best economic policy for Britain, John Healey tells the Treasury committee.

The chancellor explains:

double quotation markI went into this budget process less than four months ago, with really deep concerns about the global economic storms that we faced, which had not been reflected in the OBR spring forecast.

And now the OBR and the Bank of England are really clear – The conflict in the Middle East is driving rising energy costs, driving debt, increased costs, and it’s also weakening economic growth that’s hitting nations worldwide. But it’s hitting us particularly hard in this country.

Richard Partington

Chancellor Healey also told MPs that “I am ready to say no to data centres” if they don’t have community benefits.

He says he does not want to see a “free-for-all on data centres as we saw in the US”... but equally says pushing to win investment in AI and that development of the sector is “inevitable”.

John Healey has also revealed that UK AI chip startup Fractile has been valued at $7bn in its latest fundraising round.

The chancellor told MP that Fractile has just conducted a £500m funding round, including a contribution from the British Business Bank.

This lifted the valuation of this “British based company, British started company to $7 billion”, through the “largest ever European semiconductor funding round”, Healey adds proudly.

Fractile is developing chips designed to improve AI inference, the process through which AI models generate responses.

Tech shares are broadly higher on Wall Street in early trading, lifting the Nasdaq Composite index up by 1.2%.

CoreWeave is leading the risers, up 12%, after cheering investors with its financial results last night.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, says the AI trade is turning a corner:

double quotation markThe roller coaster ride for markets continues, and US stocks are staging a recovery today, after Tuesday’s post CPI sell off. US stocks are surging, led by Nvidia is higher by more than 2.5% so fa

Back in the tech world, Nvidia’s shares have opened higher.

After two days of falls, Nvidia’s share price is up 2% in early trading.

John Healey 'dismayed' by budget bank tax leak

Chancellor John Healey says he is “dismayed” that the details of his bank tax plans leaked on the morning of the budget.

He tells the Treasury committee that he did not want any leaks out of the budget process, and takes all leaks seriously.

Healey says he was determined as chancellor to avoid budget leaks, after seeing the damage caused by the flurry of reports ahead of the budget in 2025.

The chancellor explains:

double quotation markThere are real world impacts, not just moving the markets or the gilt yields. We saw last year with speculation, kite flying, leaks, briefings. We saw people cashing in their pension pots, where they didn’t need to. We saw people cancelling and changing investment plans when they didn’t need to.

MPs grill Treasury over bank tax leak

Over in parliament, MPs are grilling top brass from the Treasury about last month’s budget – starting with the leak of the chancellor’s bank tax plans.

Q: Was this the worst type of breach you can think of?

James Bowler, permanent secretary at the HM Treasury, says it is “deeply regrettable and frustrating” that Bloomberg had “the shape” of the bank tax on the morning of the budget, before it was announced that afternoon.

[Reminder: Bloomberg reported that the surcharge would only rise by 3 percentage points, and would be temporary]

But no, he argues it is not the worst type – it doesn’t compare to the situation last year, he argues.

Q: but was the leak an example of inside information?

Bowler replies that the market did move after the report (bank shares went up).

Chancellor John Healey steps in too, promising that the results of the investigation into the leak will be shared with this committee.

Europe’s largest energy grid operator E.ON ⁠is reviewing whether former nuclear plant sites in Germany ⁠could be ⁠converted ​into data centres.

Finance chief Nadia Jakobi told analysts today:

double quotation mark“These former power plants can provide attractive industrial locations and ‌depending on the site, we can use the existing infrastructure, ​particularly the large grid connection.

She added that E.ON is taking a “first step” with ⁠US chip designer Nvidia.

Taylor Wimpey cuts homebuilding forecast again

Taylor Wimpey, one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders, has cut its outlook for home completions for a second time this year and blamed rising mortgage and living costs – another sign of a weakening housing market.

The government’s 1.5m new homes target over five years looks even more out of reach, as the company joined others in warning of a “subdued” autumn selling season. It comes after Britain’s biggest brickmaker, Ibstock, issued a profit warning last week.

Taylor ‌Wimpey now expects to complete 10,500 homes this year, excluding joint ventures, ‌below its previous forecast of 10,600 to 10,800 homes. Adjusted operating profit is expected to be at the lower end of its £262m to £299m range. The firm also reduced its outlook in July.

Its order book declined to 6,839 homes as of 8 November, versus 7,253 a year earlier. Taylor Wimpey has also been hit by higher build cost inflation, running at 3% to 4%, due to knock-on effects from the Iran war.

Jennie Daly, the chief executive, said:

double quotation mark“The autumn selling season has been more subdued, as higher mortgage rates and living costs continue to reduce customer affordability.”

Its share price fell 4.5% in early trading and is now 3.5% lower, and dragged down rival Persimmon, which is trading 1% lower.

The Bank of England raised its base rate last week, from 3.75% to 4%, which hit mortgage borrowers but will benefit savers. The Bank’s governor, Andrew Bailey, said another hike could be needed soon, but this (partly) depends on a resolution of the Iran war and the consequent impact on energy prices and inflation.

To entice buyers, Taylor Wimpey is offering more incentives than usual, for example a deposit top-up and one-off mortgage contribution. And it has cut its selling prices by 2.5% year on year.

It said it is well positioned to participate in the government’s new Your First Home scheme aimed at first-time buyers. But the scheme won’t launch until April, and experts have warned that the market could remain sluggish until then.

Investment bank Baird has cut its rating on Nvidia’s shares to ‘neutral’, and slashed their target price for the stock, Reuters report.

Having previously predicted Nvidia could reach $500, Baird have lowered their target price to $200 (reminder, they closed at $168.89 last night).

The FT’s Unhedged column has a handy breakdown of what we know about the Nvidia crisis…

Nvidia is the indispensable supplier and, increasingly, financier of the infrastructure powering the entire AI boom;

Huang is the boom’s chief salesperson and its most influential figure who is not running one of the AI labs;

Huang is a trusted adviser to Donald Trump on the US-China AI race and AI regulation;

US intelligence has believed for months that Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang.

And some things we don’t know (but which Joon H. Kim may answer!):

Did Huang mislead Nvidia’s board? Did he disclose that he had a conflict of interest with a major and geopolitically sensitive customer?

Did the board know US intelligence suspected Alice Huang of being linked to Chinese intelligence?

Did the company know about the affair when it told The New York Times two weeks ago that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected” for the executive of an important commercial partner?

How strong is the evidence that has led US intelligence to conclude that Alice Huang is a spy

And the upshot is that removing Jensen Huang may simply be too big a risk, they suggest.

Although, as my colleague Nils Pratley wrote this week, Huang may look less powerful once the investigation has concluded…

Updated at 06.31 EST

Business.title: Federal judge allows Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against BBC to proceed
Business.text:
Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case. The president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit stems from the BBC’s splicing together of disparate comments he made before the 6 January US Capitol insurrection, as rendered in a Panorama documentary called Trump: A Second Chance.

“Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” the Trump-appointed Florida district court judge wrote. “It would be difficult for the Court to accept a different framing without completely negating the significance and fragility of political elections.”

The judge noted the significance of the documentary’s editing decision, which spliced together comments made by Trump that were nearly 55 minutes apart, something the BBC has apologized for.

“On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice,” he wrote. “BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.”

The judge continued: “Editing is often required. However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech.”

The judge noted past errors in the broadcaster’s coverage and wrote that “such examples can be said to be probative of BBC’s state of mind as it pertains to recklessness in light of BBC’s non-action toward false statements about Trump. Thus, Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump.”

The judge also wrote that “Trump’s allegations regarding BBC’s departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence”.

The BBC released a statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

Trump heralded the ruling on Truth Social, calling it a “huge victory”. “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” Trump said.

While the judge determined that Trump had “sufficiently pleaded” that the BBC acted with actual malice, the legal standard for a public figure to win a defamation case, he will have to actually prove they did so at trial.

The judge also dismissed Trump’s claim that the BBC violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

And the judge determined that the president will have to prove that he suffered “actual damages” from the airing of the document, which was not broadcast in Florida.

Business.title: US inflation rose 0.4% in October as price increases cooled and gas costs dipped
Business.text:
US inflation rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above expectations but still a cooldown in price increases as the cost of gas dipped during the month.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the usual year-over-year inflation figure as part of the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the price of a basket of goods and services, as data was not collected in October 2025 during the government shutdown.

But the newest data shows that prices are still increasing at a moderate pace. Economists estimate that, if interpolating the data for October 2025, the topline inflation figure for October 2026 would have been 3.9%, according to Oxford Economics. That would have been the highest its been since May 2026, when inflation reached 4.2%, a three-year high.

Higher energy costs driven by the Iran war have been the main factor behind increased inflation. Energy prices continued to rise slightly in October, rising 0.7% after going up 5.2% in September. In September, the overall monthly change in CPI from August was 0.6%.

The new data comes after a midterm election that will give Democrats control of Congress, in what was largely seen as a rebuke of Republicans over high prices. In their postmortem of the midterms, Republicans, including JD Vance, have specifically pointed to frustration over increased gas prices as a reason why the party fared so poorly in the election.

Gas prices cooled slightly in October, dropping from an average of $4.41 a gallon at the beginning of the month to $4.22 a gallon, prices are still more than $1 a gallon higher than a year ago, according to AAA. On Monday, the average price for a gallon at the pump fell below $4 for the first time since July.

The cost of diesel, which is used to power trucks, farming equipment, buses and trains, is nearly $2.50 a gallon higher compared with prices last year but has also been going down since October. Gas prices have continued to drop.

In September, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and are expected to hike rates again at their next meeting in December. Higher interest rates slow the economy by making borrowing money more expensive, and can slow inflation. The Fed’s target inflation rate is 2%, which it considers a stable pace for price increases.

Growth in the labor market surpassed economists’ expectations in October, giving more room for the Fed to hike rates. The unemployment rate has been relatively steady, hovering just above 4%.

Because today’s inflation is so closely tied to energy prices, it’s unclear how much and how quickly a rate hike could ease prices. But the Fed’s chair, Kevin Warsh, said the central bank is dedicated to making sure price increases ease up.

“Our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored,” Warsh said on 28 October.

Consumer sentiment increased slightly at the end of October as gas prices eased, according to the University of Michigan’s Survey of Consumers. At the same time, the US stock market was experiencing a dip as investors voiced skepticism over the influx of AI spending.

“While sentiment lifted for lower- and middle-wealth consumers, it fell 5% for those with the largest stock portfolios in the wake of ​a relatively ​turbulent period ⁠in stock markets,” said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers, in a statement. “Moreover, ​consumers’ comments revealed growing anxiety over ​a ⁠possible AI bubble.”

Sports.title: Man Utd manager: Mauricio Pochettino's decade-long courtship - but Michael Carrick deserves better
Sports.text:
When the expected formalities of Michael Carrick's dismissal as Manchester United are completed after a summit meeting in Monaco, Mauricio Pochettino looks set to turn a decade-long courtship with Old Trafford into a full-blown relationship.

Pochettino and United go back a long way, with the Argentine's name associated with the club since he was spotted leaving a lunch appointment at Scott's restaurant in Mayfair with Sir Alex Ferguson in 2016.

Ferguson was three years into his retirement, while Pochettino was building his reputation at Tottenham, where he fashioned an intense, all-out-attacking team that the great Scot admired.

Pochettino called it "a meeting in London between colleagues, between a genius and an apprentice".

In that moment, a link was forged.

Pochettino was mentioned as a contender to succeed Louis van Gaal when he was sacked by United in May 2016, then when Jose Mourinho suffered the same fate in December 2018.

Pochettino was the other name on United's shortlist when Erik ten Hag was appointed in April 2022, then again when the Dutchman was shown the door in October 2024.

Finally, as Carrick awaits what looks to be the inevitable, it looks like Pochettino will inherit the Old Trafford empire.

The problem for Pochettino is that the once great footballing empire is crumbling before the eyes, the dysfunctional product of years of poor decision-making and questionable appointments, allied to a Frankenstein's monster of a squad assembled by six managers.

One of Pochettino's quirks is to have a box of lemons in his office, believing they absorb negative energy. He will need several truckloads of the industrial strength variety to suck away the current mood at Old Trafford.

First things first, however, and that means waiting for the official confirmation of Carrick's departure, a long drawn-out affair which does little credit to part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

Carrick, 45, has proved to be out of his depth since being confirmed as permanent head coach following a successful interim spell, but his history of success as a player, his basic decency and his obvious desire to turn United's fortunes around makes the ham-fisted handling of his sacking another uncomfortable episode.

It is an emotion reflected by United's increasingly disaffected fanbase, who have made it clear who they blame for their current place in the Premier League relegation zone.

Pochettino's appointment would land in the middle ground between the flawed sentimentalism of turning to fan favourites with little or no track record of success, such as Carrick and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, as well as the quick fix of bringing in proven past winners such as Van Gaal and Mourinho.

With his one-time dream of returning to Spurs now seemingly out of reach forever, Pochettino is ready to pick up the reins at the fallen giants that are United, another club he has clearly always had in his sights.

He is currently coach of the USA, whom he led at this summer's World Cup, but even then United were lurking on his agenda.

During the campaign Pochettino held court with invited journalists at the USA team hotel in California.

When mention was made of United, Pochettino turned to his closest confidante and ever-present assistant coach Jesus Perez to say: "One day, your dream comes true. You go to Manchester United."

Perez replied with "United should have got you", promoting the response from a smiling Pochettino: "Future. Future."

Now the future is here.

The big question now is what Pochettino will United be getting?

He remains a beloved figure at Spurs, where he had an outstanding record of consistency following his appointment from Southampton in May 2014.

He never finished lower than fifth - in his first season - in any full campaign in charge, including second place behind Chelsea in 2016-17 and third in 2015-16 and 2017-18.

The one question mark always placed against Pochettino, including when he finished sixth at Chelsea in 2023-24, was an inability to get his teams over the line to tangible success in England.

Pochettino claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with Paris St-Germain after leaving Spurs - the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title - but the club's hierarchy felt that was the minimum he should achieve given the squad at his disposal, and he did not see out his contract.

In England with Spurs, he was runner-up in the League Cup in 2014-15 and reached the FA Cup semi-finals in 2016-17 and 2017-18. In 2018-19 he reached the Champions League final and the League Cup semis.

In one season at Chelsea - a loveless relationship in which he could never shed his Spurs connections in the eyes of fans - he reached the FA Cup semi-finals and lost the League Cup final.

Pochettino's driven, competitive nature means that is an itch he will want to scratch when his United appointment is confirmed.

While Spurs have always appeared to be his first love, there is also no doubt United occupies a special place in his thoughts.

Spanish football expert Guillem Balague, who worked with Pochettino on his book Brave New World, says: "There is a fit with the people at the club too.

"Omar Berrada is a fan. When Manchester City drew up a shortlist to replace Pep Guardiola, some City supporters, including Omar, argued for Pochettino to be on it.

"There are plenty of clues about his feelings for United in the book. He was at the stadium in 1999 when United won the Champions League.

"Sir Alex Ferguson is mentioned 28 times, more than any other name in the biography.

"Spurs tried to push back and cut those references. Pochettino and I talked it over and decided that none of it would be touched. That shows how much it mattered to him."

Pochettino is a renowned builder, as he proved at Spurs after succeeding the sacked Tim Sherwood, working with Harry Kane to develop the recently crowned Ballon d'Or winner, as well as bringing Son Heung-Min to the club for a bargain £22m from Bayer Leverkusen in 2015.

If Pochettino can repeat that - a tough job in United's circumstances - and reproduce the easy-on-the-eye, attacking football played with relentless energy, then he could finally be the perfect fit Ratcliffe has so far looked in vain to discover.

Pochettino is also his own man, so it will be intriguing to see how he works with Ratcliffe, Berrada and Wilcox.

The road to Pochettino's sacking at Spurs effectively started following a friendly win against Real Madrid only weeks after their Champions League final defeat, when he made it clear he was not having enough influence at the club.

He enjoys warm relationships with his players, with a track record of improvement. It was no co-incidence that Cole Palmer enjoyed his best season working under Pochettino at Chelsea, scoring 25 goals in 45 appearances.

Pochettino, however, is also single-minded and ruthless, as he proved with an emphatic response to criticism for not phoning the players he left out of the USA World Cup squad.

He said: "When I was a player, when I didn't make the roster I didn't want my coach to call me. The players who didn't make the roster, they don't want to hear me say 'I apologise'. What are you going to say? Am I going to lie?"

He will need to call on every one of those qualities if and when he assumes control at United.

Back to that lunch date with Ferguson.

The final word on that day went to Pochettino as the pair argued over who was picking up the tab.

Ferguson said Pochettino could pay if he named an Argentina player who scored in the 1930 World Cup final.

Pochettino, in what he claimed was a moment of inspiration, named Guillermo Stabile.

He won that argument. Now both he and Ferguson will hope Pochettino can produce more moments of inspiration to win something more substantial at United.

Pochettino and United go back a long way, with the Argentine's name...

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Michael Carrick.
Sports.text:
Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach.

United have opened talks with the Argentine about him potentially replacing Michael Carrick, who is expected to be relieved of his duties in the next 48 hours.

Once Carrick's future is clarified, sources have told BBC Sport that USA manager Pochettino wants to take the job.

US Soccer officials are expecting an official approach from United - and sources have told BBC Sport they have a contingency plan for their manager leaving, which includes a succession plan.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino wants to remain respectful to the US Soccer Federation and will wait for United to make their approach.

The Red Devils would be required to pay $10m (£7.5m) to release Pochettino from his contract, which he only signed in August.

The USA have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week.

With confidence over a succession plan, it raises the possibility that Pochettino may not take charge of those games.

On Thursday, US Soccer cancelled planned media with players citing a clash with Veterans Day, though some reports claimed it was to stop the squad being asked about their manager.

Pochettino, 54, is understood to view the prospect of managing United as a serious opportunity, with the expectation being he would accept the job were it formally offered.

United have spoken to the ex-Argentina defender about their managerial position on three previous occasions - when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 before the club appointed Erik ten Hag and again when the Dutchman was sacked in 2024.

Carrick's future at United will be decided at a meeting in Monaco on Wednesday that will be attended by chief executive Omar Berrada, director of football Jason Wilcox and co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Berrada and Wilcox have flown to Monaco for one of their regular, planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.

On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.

It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.

Carrick, 45, was pictured arriving at the club's Carrington training base on Wednesday.

United are 18th in the Premier League - inside the relegation zone - after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August.

It is the club's lowest position at this stage of a top-flight season since 1986-87, when they were 20th.

Pochettino's first job in the Premier League was at Southampton from January 2013, before a five-year stint at Tottenham from 2014 that included a Champions League final appearance.

He managed Paris St-Germain from January 2021 to July 2022 before spending the 2023-24 season in charge of Chelsea.

Pochettino moved into international football by taking the USA job in September 2024, and led the co-hosts to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup.

While it may seem a touch immoral for Manchester United to be talking to a potential new manager before they have decided if their current one is staying or not, this kind of situation is not uncommon in football.

Jose Mourinho had agreed a contract with United in 2016 before Louis van Gaal was sacked, which is how stories - including from BBC Sport - came out that the Dutchman would be dismissed as he was celebrating the FA Cup final triumph over Crystal Palace.

Going further back, Mark Hughes was replaced immediately by Roberto Mancini at Manchester City in 2009. Hughes' imminent dismissal was reported on the morning of his final game in charge.

It is impossible to reach that situation without talks taking place beforehand, and it would be naive to think they do not go on in a world in which agents are pushing clients for jobs that either do, or do not, exist or clubs are trying to gauge interest before making a decision.

I have been told by one source the Pochettino terms to join United are more or less agreed. I have also been told if they decide to push on, United can decide whether the former Spurs and Chelsea boss remains with the USA team for their matches against Haiti.

If he did stay, it would mean a sharp turnaround from a Tuesday night match - which finishes in the early hours of Wednesday - to be at Carrington for preparations before United's game against Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.

There are a lot of gaps to fill in yet, not least whether Carrick will be dismissed or not.

But it seems more likely there will be clarity on that on Wednesday, and from that the rest of the jigsaw pieces should start to slot into place.

Sports.title: Harry Kane: How England captain's 'fairytale' came true as he closes in on appearance record
Sports.text:
"It's great when fairytales come true," England boss Roy Hodgson said after 21-year-old Tottenham striker Harry Kane scored 79 seconds into his international debut back in 2015.

"Let's hope it's the start of a good and long England career for him."

Eleven years on, Kane will make his 126th appearance for his country and become the most-capped men's player in Three Lions history when England play Croatia in the Nations League at Wembley on Thursday (19:45 GMT).

Peter Shilton, who served England as a goalkeeper, won 125 caps between 1970 and 1990.

"It's not about me - it's about the team," said Kane, scorer of 91 goals in 125 appearances for his country, about his landmark moment.

"I love coming to every England camp, I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible."

Kane, 33, has gone through every emotion playing for his country.

He fought back tears after missing a penalty in the World Cup quarter-final defeat by France in 2022, and sang Wonderwall with fans following the win over Croatia at this summer's World Cup - which he labelled one of his "favourite ever moments" in a Three Lions shirt.

London-born Kane is the boy who grew up in Chingford to captain his country, become England's record goalscorer and win the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Now the Bayern Munich striker stands on the brink of making more appearances than any other man in England's football history.

"He wins the Ballon d'Or, and deservedly so, and in the next game for England he gets the all-time record with 126 matches," England boss Thomas Tuchel said about Kane when announcing his squad last week.

"Thursday is a deserved occasion to celebrate an extraordinary player."

Long before Kane made his first senior appearance for his country in a 4-0 Euro 2015 qualifying win over Lithuania at Wembley, he was an England fan.

Aged 12, he remembers the heartache of going out on penalties to Portugal in the quarter-finals of the 2006 World Cup under Sven-Goran Eriksson and failing to qualify for Euro 2008 under Steve McClaren.

"During most major tournaments we would go to the pub to watch England, with the beer garden and the screen," said Kane.

"We loved England, we loved watching England and we were big England fans. I remember many tears being shed after we went out on penalties and things like that."

Kane fell in love with football from an early age.

Aged five, he wrote about his ambition to become a footballer in a school project.

Weekends and holidays were spent playing football in his local Ridgeway Park with his dad Patrick and brother Charlie.

They would use trees as goalposts, with the two brothers taking turns to shoot while Patrick was in goal.

Wayne Rooney was England captain and Joe Hart was goalkeeper when Kane came on to make his Three Lions debut 11 years ago.

"My reaction when he first came into the England squad was: 'Alright, who is this guy?'" Hart told BBC Sport of the young Tottenham striker called up after scoring 26 goals in 42 league and cup games in 2014-15.

"Then I was like: 'Oh OK, he's good! Then he kept coming back [into the England squad] and my reaction was: 'Flipping heck, he's getting better!'

"I went to Tottenham during Covid and it got to the point in training where he was that good that I wasn't even diving for his shots. I was thinking: 'I adore you, but you are frustrating the life out of me.'"

Kane's rise from Leyton Orient loan signing to Ballon d'Or winner is well-documented.

His story - the model student and family man who married his childhood sweetheart and became an England great - serves as a reminder to pupils at his old school to never give up on their dreams.

He has not forgotten his roots - or the clubs that helped him on his pathway.

In 2020, Kane sponsored Leyton Orient's shirt. The club's home strip carried a message of thanks to frontline workers tackling the coronavirus pandemic.

Mental health charity Mind and Haven House Children's Hospice also had their logos on Orient's two change shirts as part of the deal.

"I was born and brought up only a couple of miles from Orient's stadium and I'm really happy to have the opportunity to give back to the club that gave me my first professional start," said Kane at the time.

"It also gives me a platform to say a big thank you to the many frontline heroes and charities out there who provide care and support during these challenging times."

Matthaus, who has witnessed Kane's impact at Bayern Munich, added: "He is a good person, a good ambassador, the captain of the English national team playing at a German club."

On Thursday, England's players and fans will salute Kane for breaking another record and making it 126 not out.

"He is superhuman," added Hart.

Sports.title: Man City: Are Enzo Maresca's side's issues psychological or tactical?
Sports.text:
The ongoing international break will give Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca much-needed time to fix the growing issues in his squad.

The Italian made a dream start after taking over from Pep Guardiola in the summer, leading the club to a record seven consecutive victories at the beginning of the Premier League season.

But three consecutive defeats have followed as they have fallen six points adrift of league leaders Arsenal, who are looking in imperious form as they aim to retain their title.

In September, it was announced that City had been found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, and matches have continued as the club await the outcome of their appeal.

With possible sanctions hanging over them, is City's recent league form down to psychological issues or are there tactical problems Maresca needs to address?

Renowned sports psychologist Dr Paul McCarthy has 25 years' experience working in the industry with top clubs in England, Scotland, Germany and France.

McCarthy works on the personal and professional lives of players and says both contribute to how well they perform on the pitch, with the need to "piece together a jigsaw" when situations become disrupted.

"Players are like everyone else - they talk about what is going on in their own lives and things that are topical, especially about uncertain events," McCarthy tells BBC Sport.

"It generates communication with a lot of stories and rumour and over time if there are enough losses, there often becomes a reduced collective efficacy.

"A collective efficacy is a squad's belief in their ability to do what they need to do [to win] and because of their success in the past, that is often shaken a little by consecutive losses."

City were sitting pretty at the top of the table after a flawless start, but have dropped to third - behind Arsenal and Brighton.

After the guilty verdict was announced during the last international break, Maresca's men won their first game back - against 10-man Liverpool at Anfield - then narrowly overcame Ipswich at Etihad Stadium in their following match.

But they have since lost to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest, with defensive issues exposed and individual mistakes proving costly.

In their first seven games of the season, City did not concede any goals because of individual errors - but that has shifted dramatically in the past three matches, with four mistakes from players contributing to goals.

City have conceded 13 goals after 10 league games - their highest total at this stage of a season since 2008-09, when they had let in 16 - and that has prompted questions about their defensive solidity.

Asked if the uncertainty over the ongoing appeal process may affect the focus and attention of players, McCarthy said: "Yeah, that would be a very reasonable human response.

"When people are uncertain about their future, that uncertainty leads to a lack of perceived control, so uncertainty is often more stressful than bad news and the research shows that.

"So while you are waiting and you don't know the outcome, you are uncertain of where you are and there is that lack of control for a lot of people - they come to training, they play their games and it's outside of their responsibility."

While at Chelsea, in a video for NBC Sports, Maresca discussed his tactics - moving counters into a 3-2-2-3 shape before pushing one up to create the 3-1-6 shape.

He explained using six attackers was a tactic he had employed against Inter Milan to outnumber their back five.

This season, he has adopted the 3-1-6 shape more permanently - trading a second holding midfielder for an extra attacking midfielder.

Coaching a team full of quality footballers, there is logic to wanting to play in a more front-footed and imposing manner, but how well tactics are performed depend on the skillset of the players asked to do them.

The big questions come in the form of Elliot Anderson and his midfield partners.

Anderson - naturally more of a roaming midfielder - leans on his physical strengths. At Nottingham Forest, he defended intensely, pressed high and wide, and contributed to attacks. This season, Maresca and his staff have looked to mould him into more of a sitting midfielder after the departure of Rodri in the summer.

Learning that role will take time, as it did for Rodri when he first joined.

It is not problematic in its own right to try to coach a player into a key role, but City have looked exposed through the middle of the pitch more often in recent games.

Anderson, who has largely impressed, has played to his habit - stepping out of a holding midfield position to attempt to press or track opposition players, often looking to win the ball back. Clever opponents have used this to drag him out of position before finding players through the middle.

For Maresca, the issue is less around the shape, and more around losing the ball in the first instance. After the loss to Forest, he said: "You concede transitions when you lose the ball, and when you don't win duels."

Further concerns arise when assessing the skillset of the players behind Anderson.

Gianluigi Donnarumma is not a goalkeeper renowned for his ball-playing ability. The defensive cohort are serviceable on the ball but have made costly errors under pressure, playing out from the back, this season too.

Guardiola's solution to mitigate some of these issues last season came in the form of asking midfielders to shoulder more ball-playing responsibility.

The loss of Rodri and especially Bernardo Silva, who would drop deep and take City from their own goal into midfield alone, have made City's problems more obvious.

As good as Anderson is, he is not a player who can single-handedly resolve build-up play as Bernardo Silva did, but Ayyoub Bouaddi may be somebody that could be used in this manner as we saw him against Brazil's press in the World Cup.

Sports.title: Emma Raducanu to return at United Cup in January after lengthy injury absence
Sports.text:
Emma Raducanu will make her return to tennis in the United Cup team competition in Australia in the first week of 2027.

Britain's 2021 US Open champion has not played since June because of a stress fracture of the shin.

Raducanu was beaten by Croatia’s Donna Vekic in her first grass-court final at Queen's Club on 14 June, but had to pull out of Wimbledon on the eve of her opening match just 14 days later.

The 23-year-old contemplated playing a couple of events in Asia this autumn but, by delaying her return until January, she will be able to use a special ranking of 38 to enter tournaments.

A special ranking is available to players who have been out with injury for at least six months. In Raducanu's case, it reflects her position in the world rankings after Wimbledon, as she received some prize money despite not playing a match there.

The current British number five will be able to use a special ranking to enter eight events next year, including two Grand Slams and five WTA 1000 tournaments.

Her actual ranking of 107 would likely be too low to make the main draw of January's Australian Open and most other WTA Tour events.

But with a special ranking, Raducanu will not only be assured of playing in Melbourne but also at the WTA 1000 events in Doha, Dubai, Indian Wells and Miami which follow in February and March.

The entry deadline for the United Cup passed on Monday, shortly after Raducanu had her application for a special ranking approved.

A ranking of 38 will make her the British number one for the purposes of this event, giving her the chance to play alongside Arthur Fery in a competition featuring 18 national teams.

Francesca Jones, Jan Choinski and doubles players Neal Skupski and Olivia Nicholls complete the British team for the tournament, which takes place from 1-10 January.

Britain will play Australia and France in their group matches in Sydney, and Raducanu can expect to be face current top-40 players Talia Gibson and Diane Parry.

Raducanu made a gradual return to training in early September - and four months is a long time to train without any competitive action.

She may also not play any exhibitions between now and the end of the year but a spell of warm weather training is anticipated, with the Middle East a popular destination for players in the run-up to the Australian Open.

Recent practice sessions in London with head coach Andrew Richardson and LTA national coach Alex Ward have been increasing in intensity, according to observers.

But by the time Raducanu returns, she will have been on the sidelines for over six months. Playing a few tournaments in Asia would have helped her regain some match sharpness, and perhaps allowed for a faster start to 2027.

Her fellow Briton Sonay Kartal is a fine example, having enjoyed considerable success since returning from six months out with a stress fracture of the back in September.

After reaching the third round of the China Open in her first WTA Tour event back, she beat world number six Elina Svitolina and then world number 12 Belinda Bencic on her way to the Wuhan Open final.

Kartal says there were a "lot of conversations" about where she should make a return.

"I think I wanted to just go straight in. I trusted that I would be able to get my level back, I just didn't know how quickly," the 25-year-old said.

"But I still think there is a long way to go. I can produce the level, but can I sustain it?

"Rehab is draining, and the body is not used to a lot of matches on the tour, so I do feel the aches and the pains from that."

There will only be 24 candles on Raducanu’s birthday cake later this week, but there is no escaping the amount of time she has missed since her stunning New York victory as a teenage qualifier.

She has averaged just 31 matches a season in the five years since that triumph. Players with aspirations to be inside the world's top 20 would hope to play around twice that number.

Elena Rybakina, for example, played 68 matches across 20 tournaments this year as she rose to the top of the world rankings for the first time.

By contrast, Raducanu played just 21 matches, losing in the second round of the Australian Open and the first round at Roland Garros.

Last year, Raducanu contested a career-best 50 matches, and earlier this year rose to 23 in the rankings shortly after reaching the final in the Romanian city of Cluj.

But her early preparation was affected by bone bruising of the foot, and she did not play for two months between March and May because of a post-viral illness picked up in Cluj.

Raducanu said a stress fracture of the shin was only confirmed after a final scan on the night before Wimbledon. But in her desperation to play, she had continued to train at times in the run-up to the championships, when medical advice had suggested that might be unwise.

Sports.title: England v Japan: Eddie Jones sets sights on chaos and upset
Sports.text:
Head coach Eddie Jones says Japan are drawing inspiration from Italy, who beat England for the first time in March, as the Brave Blossoms attempt to heap pressure back on Steve Borthwick with their own landmark win on Saturday.

Jones was sacked by England in December 2022 after a miserable autumn which ended in a 27-13 Twickenham defeat by South Africa and jeers from the home fans.

The Australian, 66, hopes to cause similar unrest on his return to Allianz Stadium this weekend.

"We're massive underdogs," Jones told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We've got to find a way to disrupt an England side that's looking at New Zealand next week [England play the All Blacks on 21 November] and sometimes may be a little bit distracted.

"Our opportunity is to get in there, cause some havoc, cause some chaos, put off their game, get the crowd booing. Then the sky starts to come in on Twickenham and you never know what can happen.

"We've seen it happen with Italy and other countries."

Japan have lost all six of their previous Test meetings with England, most recently going down 54-19 on their autumn visit two years ago.

However Italy, who won for the first time in 33 attempts earlier this year, and Fiji, who broke their duck with a 30-22 success in 2023, have both secured maiden victories over England during Borthwick's reign.

Jones believes England's players are uniquely susceptible to pressure, given a level of scrutiny which is unprecedented in the rest of the global game.

A run of five successive defeats earlier this year, combined with reports of a rift between players and coaches, raised the stakes for England before Sunday's meeting with Australia.

However, Borthwick's players, who had insisted that the squad remains united, delivered an impressive 45-22 victory to vindicate their coach.

"The noise does get to the team and it can be pretty loud in England," said Jones, for whom Borthwick worked as an assistant during a previous stint with Japan and then with England.

"You've got a lot of newspapers, a lot of media, probably more than any other country in the world. Sometimes that can weigh down on the players and it's the job of the leadership to get the players thinking straight.

"Steve's an outstanding coach and a very intelligent man, and a really good coach. So I've got the highest respect for him."

Sports.title: Tom O'Brien: Jockey dies aged 39 after cancer diagnosis
Sports.text:
Jockey Tom O'Brien has died at the age of 39 after being diagnosed with cancer.

Irishman O'Brien rode more than 1,000 winners in Britain and Ireland, including two at the Cheltenham Festival and the Welsh Grand National twice.

The nephew of trainer Aidan O'Brien, he was a mainstay of the Minehead operation run by Philip Hobbs, joining as a teenager and remaining until his retirement in 2023.

"He touched countless lives on both sides of the Irish Sea, bringing joy to everyone who had the privilege of knowing him and watching what he did best, on and off the racecourse," said British Horseracing Authority (BHA) chief executive Brant Dunshea.

"Tom was held in the highest esteem and meant so much to so many people across our sport, who benefitted from his kindness and loyal friendship.

"He will be hugely missed and his loss is immensely difficult to process.

"The racing family is distraught, but I know how we will all rally round to provide each other with support, comfort and to remember Tom as we knew him best: a brilliant jockey, a valued colleague, a loyal friend and above all a loving husband and devoted father."

Riding the Hobbs-trained Thyme Hill, O'Brien won the Liverpool Hurdle in 2021 and the Kauto Star Novices' Chase in 2022.

"It's very sad, particularly for his wife Hayley and two young children," said Hobbs, who now shares Minehead with Johnson White.

"He came to our yard from Ireland having not ridden in a race, but it soon became obvious he was pretty talented.

"He was always very reliable and a very good bloke. There's lots of good memories and there were lots of winners.

"I'd kept in touch with Tom since his retirement as he only lived half an hour away. He was only in our yard about three weeks ago."

O'Brien joined the BHA stewarding team after ending his racing career.

Sports.title: Tatjana Smith switches allegiance from South Africa to Netherlands
Sports.text:
South Africa's most decorated Olympian Tatjana Smith was in tears as she announced that she has switched allegiance to the Netherlands.

The 29-year-old won four Olympic breaststroke medals, including two golds, before retiring after the Paris 2024 Games.

She came out of retirement in September and hopes to compete in the 50m breaststroke as the event makes its Olympic debut at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.

Smith, whose maiden name was Schoenmaker, wiped away tears as she read a letter addressed to South Africa, saying that "dreams can change as we grow".

Smith has dual citizenship because her father is Dutch.

She said she has "always been Dutch and South African" and that this is an opportunity to "explore another part of my identity and heritage that I've never experienced through sport".

She said it also offers her "greater high-performance support and the potential to build a more sustainable career" because the "financial and practical challenges of swimming were among the reasons my previous career became difficult to sustain".

Smith has previously said that financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, contributed to her decision to step away from the sport.

Swimming South Africa has been approached for comment.

Smith won four world and Commonwealth gold medals between 2018 and 2023.

She won gold in the 200m breaststroke and 100m silver at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, before adding 100m gold and 200m silver in 2024.

"Representing South Africa was a childhood dream come true, and it's a chapter I will always look back on with immense pride and gratitude," she said on social media., external

"The people, the memories and everything we achieved together will always be part of me. But dreams can change as we grow.

"This next chapter is about embracing another part of who I am, falling in love with the journey and discovering what more I'm capable of.

"I'm excited for what lies ahead, and I truly hope you'll continue to be part of the journey with me."

Smith, who said she will continue to live and train in South Africa, is set to represent the Netherlands for the first time at the short course World Championships from 1-6 December.

She acknowledged that her switch "may disappoint or break the hearts" of some supporters.

The Ministry of Sport, Arts and Culture in South Africa said it was aware of the "problems at Swimming South Africa".

"The country was delighted to see her return to the pool, but South Africa does not own her," a statement read.

"Tatjana's choice belongs to her and it should not be turned into a political weapon."

Gayton McKenzie, Minister of Sports, Arts and Culture, said: "Every medal, every record and every anthem she gave us belongs to our history forever. We now have to share her with the Netherlands."

Sports.title: Ronnie O'Sullivan loses 4-0 to Shaun Murphy at Champion of Champions
Sports.text:
Seven-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan suffered a 4-0 defeat by Shaun Murphy at the Champion of Champions tournament in Leicester.

Murphy, the 2005 world champion, lost this year's World Championship final in a deciding frame to Wu Yize.

But he will not meet Wu in the Champion of Champions last eight after the world champion lost to Chinese compatriot Chang Bingyu 4-3 in the other Group Three match.

O'Sullivan, who has been struggling for form, was playing for the first time since losing to Ka Wai Cheung at the Northern Ireland Open last month.

The 50-year-old found himself 2-0 down against Murphy, who knocked in a 68 in the second frame.

Murphy made a 41 break to take the next frame before triumphing in a tense fourth frame 61-42 to secure victory and a spot in the last eight.

Chang, his opponent in the quarter-finals, opened with a 109 break against Wu and, after losing the following three frames, reeled off three in a row himself to win.

Sports.title: Football: MP calls for heading in training to be legally restricted
Sports.text:
An MP is calling for legal safeguards to limit repetitive heading in football training, amid growing concerns about the risk of brain injury.

Grahame Morris, the Labour MP for Easington, submitted a parliamentary motion on Tuesday urging the government to take action to reduce the number of times a player can head the ball in training.

Researchers have found footballers are three and a half times more likely to die from a neurodegenerative disease than the general population.

The Early Day Motion (EDM) describes the need to protect players' brain health as a "significant public health and player welfare issue".

"The aim of this EDM is to raise awareness of the growing body of evidence linking repeated head impacts, particularly from heading a football, to an increased risk of neurodegenerative disease," Morris told BBC Sport.

The motion encourages the government "to take a more active role in prevention, education and player protection" Morris added.

Morris's motion supports a national petition submitted in September by the charity Head Safe Football, and calls on the government to take a number of actions:

Impose legal limits on repetitive heading in football training

Establish a cross-departmental task-force involving medical experts, players representatives, campaign groups and football authorities to develop "enforceable heading safeguards"

Recognise chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) as a public health concern

Create a national action plan to protect players' brain health

Improve education and awareness of the risks associated with heading, including in schools and through the PE national curriculum

EDMs are seen as a means for MPs to express their opinion on a subject and to canvass support for their views. No matter how many MPs sign up to an EDM there is no guarantee that it will be debated in Parliament.

Football does already have restrictions around heading.

The Football Association has phased out deliberate heading in grassroots football matches for children aged 11 and under.

It has also issued guidance recommending limits on heading during training of no more than 10 headers per week at amateur level.

In the professional game in England, clubs have been advised to limit players to 10 "high force" headers a week in training.

Scotland has gone further, banning heading in training on the day before and after matches in the professional game.

However, campaigners such as Dr Judith Gates, founder of Head Safe Football, believe that voluntary guidance is not enough.

"What we are finding is that coaches and parents don't know of the guidance, or the ban. Or they do not know why it exists," she told BBC Sport.

"There needs to be greater clarity and greater specific restrictions in order to protect players of today and tomorrow."

Dr Gates, whose husband the former Middlesbrough player Bill died with CTE, a degenerative brain disease associated with repeated head impacts, accepts that enforcing a legal limit would be challenging.

The calls for greater protection came as Prime Minister Andy Burnham called, in an interview with the Telegraph,, external on English football to formally recognise the game's dementia crisis and establish an "industrial injuries" compensation scheme for former players.

In a statement to BBC Sport, he said: "I've spoken to families affected by dementia and brain injury and heard what they have been through.

"Their determination to get this issue taken seriously has been extraordinary, and they should never have had to fight so hard to be heard."

Burnham's intervention follows inquests into the deaths of former England World Cup winner Nobby Stiles and Scotland defender Gordon McQueen, which found repetitive heading had contributed to their deaths.

The Professional Footballer's association (PFA) and the Premier League set up a brain health fund which has provided about £1m annually since 2023. However, campaigners say this is not enough to meet the costs of care.

The Football Association has not financially contributed to the fund, but said it continued to invest in research and had introduced guidance across professional and grassroots football.

"While the link between heading in football and long-term brain health remains the subject of ongoing scientific and medical research, we have consistently been at the forefront of efforts to help improve the safety of our game," an FA spokesperson said.

Sports.title: Women's Ashes: England to prepare with red-ball matches at home
Sports.text:
England have cancelled their scheduled Test in the West Indies in April and will instead prepare for the Women's Ashes with a number of red-ball matches in the UK.

Nat Sciver-Brunt's side have played just one Test - a heavy defeat by India at Lord's - since their last four-day meeting with Australia in January 2025, which they lost by an innings in Melbourne.

Next summer's Test against Australia, which is worth four points in the multi-format series, will be held at Headingley from 24-27 June.

England will prepare for that with four red-ball matches. One of the games will be a three-day fixture against Australia A before three intra-squad 'best v best' matches.

In addition, a dedicated red-ball training camp will be held in Bangalore in January.

England expect to use 26 or 27 players across the different training camps and matches.

It means England's schedule in the West Indies has been revised to three T20s and three one-day internationals only.

The change comes after it was suggested the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) might need to offer financial support to Cricket West Indies (CWI) to allow the Test to take place.

"We would welcome any assistance of our much wealthier member boards," CWI chief executive Chris Dehring previously told BBC Sport. "It is very expensive to host cricket in the Caribbean."

However, BBC Sport understands the ECB's decision is not related to those financial discussions and the schedule change is viewed as a performance decision in line with giving England the best chance of winning the Ashes.

West Indies have not played a women's Test since 2004, which was their only red-ball match in 47 years.

"A 10-day warm-weather red-ball camp in India followed by four further matches in English conditions will provide Charlotte Edwards and her team with the appropriate game time to be ready for that challenge [of Australia]," said ECB chief executive Richard Gould.

"Best versus best in English conditions provides a valuable opportunity for the team.

"It also allows us to assess our strength in depth, give opportunities to more players and get a number of competitive multi-day cricket matches across a longer period into the wider group."

Sports.title: NFL trade deadline winners and losers: Vikings go full dadcore with Kirk Cousins in Super Bowl quest
Sports.text:
The Vikings get the QB they desperately need

After what happened Monday night, the Minnesota Vikings had to do this. In a dispiriting loss to the Buffalo Bills, the Vikings saw their tremendous defense go to waste, as Carson Wentz completed eight of 25 passes for 81 yards, no touchdowns, two interceptions and a passer rating of 8.9. It was one of the worst quarterback performances in recent history, and it continued a run of recent QB futility for the Vikings, from JJ McCarthy to Kyler Murray to Wentz. Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores is out-scheming every other coach in the league with his laboratory of blitzes and coverages. But it’s starting to matter less and less, because opposing offenses know they can wait that defense out when there’s no juice on the other side of the ball. The Vikings rank first in scoring defense (116 points allowed), but they’re 27th in points scored (146).

This is not sustainable, which is why Minnesota welcomed ur-suburban dad Kirk Cousins back to the team he led from 2018 to 2023 by sending a 2027 third-round pick to the Las Vegas Raiders. The 38-year-old is in his 15th NFL season, and he’s not quite the player he used to be, but he’s a massive improvement over everyone else in the Vikings building at his position. This season, Cousins has completed 202 of 315 passes for 2,340 yards, 20 touchdowns, eight interceptions and a passer rating of 97.1. The rest of the Vikings QBs this season have combined for 137 of 225 passes for 1,286 yards, eight touchdowns, five interceptions and a passer rating of 82.0.

Cousins enters an NFC North that may be the most brutally competitive division in NFL history, but if he plays as he has this season so far, the Vikings have more than a puncher’s chance.

Do the Vikings like that? We suspect that they do. And in addition to his play on the field, he should bring a maturity and calm to the quarterback position in Minnesota, something critics of McCarthy and Murray say they have lacked at points during their careers.

As for the Raiders, they essentially pick up a free third-rounder after signing Cousins to a one-year, $11.3m fully guaranteed contract, and selecting Indiana quarterback Fernando Mendoza with the first overall pick in the 2026 draft. The plan all along was for Cousins to start until Mendoza was ready for the rigors of the NFL. We’re about to see if he is.

The Bears go all-in (and win) with the Jeffery Simmons trade

It usually takes a minute for a traded player, no matter how good he may be, to make a considerable difference with his new team. That player has to deal with a new city, teammates and schemes – it’s not an easy adjustment. But when the Chicago Bears traded 2027 and 2028 first-round draft picks and a 2027 fourth-rounder to the Tennessee Titans for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round draft pick … well, it cost a lot, but it made Chicago’s defense better – immediately. Per SumerSports, the Bears have gone from 6.39 yards per play allowed to 4.45 with Simmons on the field, and he’s made other Chicago defenders better, from edge rusher (and former Mississippi State teammate) Montez Sweat to linebacker Devin Bush.

In Chicago’s 27-24 Sunday night win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, that defense took over, as the usually potent Bears offense had its issues against the Bucs’ top-tier defense. Caleb Williams threw four interceptions, and Chicago won a game in which they committed five or more turnovers for the first time since they did so twice in the 2006 season – including a 24-23 win over the Arizona Cardinals that led to the greatest postgame press conference ever, courtesy of Cardinals head coach Dennis Green.

With the offense playing at its usual pace and the defense at an entirely new level, the Simmons trade is a prime example of what a big-time trade should do: turn a good team into a great one.

Seattle’s Quenton Nelson trade may hit its own unfortunate deadline

The Seattle Seahawks needed to revive a run game that has been below average since the team let last season’s Super Bowl MVP, Kenneth Walker III, walk to the Kansas City Chiefs. They believed they could solve their rushing problem by sending a 2027 third-round draft pick and a 2028 fifth-round draft pick to the Indianapolis Colts for offensive guard Quenton Nelson, the eight-time Pro Bowler who will eventually find his way to the Hall of Fame.

Nelson still has plenty to offer at the age of 30. But these deals don’t always work out the way teams hope. Seattle’s first game with Nelson was a 34-17 loss to the Bears, who came into Lumen Field with Simmons in tow and wrecked any offensive plans the Seahawks had. Nelson is a left guard, which meant that the Seahawks moved 2025 first-round pick Grey Zabel to the right side, where he hadn’t played since 2023, when he was at North Dakota State.

Moving from one side to the other is never as easy for offensive linemen as people may think, and the Bears wisely lined Simmons up more on Zabel’s side than Nelson’s – 88% to 12%, per Pro Football Focus. This allowed Simmons and his energized cohorts to pressure Sam Darnold ceaselessly, and the quarterback is now out with a quadriceps injury and a cracked rib.

Backup Drew Lock started Seattle’s win over the Arizona Cardinals last week, and Zabel moved back to the left side, because Nelson is now recovering from a knee procedure and is week-to-week.

Why is this a problem? Because Nelson won’t have time to acclimate to his new line, and Zabel won’t have time to acclimate to his new right side. Plus, Nelson is in the final year of the four-year, $80m contract extension he signed in 2022. If Nelson misses significant time, and the 5-4 Seahawks can’t find their way into the playoffs, whatever positive effects Nelson’s acquisition might have provided will be meaningless in the long term.

The Jaguars go all-in with big deals

It has become more than apparent that the Jacksonville Jaguars are all-in this season. Which makes sense. The 6-2 Jags lead the NFL in point differential (plus-108) and turnover differential (plus-9), and after their 33-10 win over the Baltimore Ravens last Thursday, they rank first overall in DVOA for the first time in the history of the franchise – which goes back to 1995.

Which is why general manager James Gladstone made the call to trade a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Atlanta Falcons for safety Jessie Bates III. Jacksonville have been assembling their safety rotation with spit and baling wire of late and have a lot of injuries to deal with, and Bates is one of the NFL’s better and more versatile players at his position(s). He’s an expert defender everywhere from the box to the slot to the deep third.

The Jags also traded a sixth-round pick for New Orleans Saints interior defensive lineman Davon Godchaux. This also works because the 6ft 3in, 330lb Godchaux is a good rotational run defender, and the Jags recently lost DaVon Hamilton, the heartbeat of their run defense, to a season-ending injury.

But as it turns out, those moves were just the opening acts. Gladstone then made a massive deal with the Philadelphia Eagles, trading a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick for defensive lineman Jordan Davis.

And this is where Gladstone and the Jaguars may be a bit over their skis.

Selected with the 13th overall pick in the 2022 draft out of Georgia, Davis was a highly-regarded interior disruptor based on his college work, but that promise never quite developed in the ways in which the Eagles hoped. The 6ft 6in, 336lbs Davis has all the athleticism and power you’d want, but the results have been middling to disappointing. Davis has never amassed more than five sacks and 28 pressures in a season. Those totals both came in 2025, after which the Eagles signed him to a three-year, $78m contract extension.

Davis has become an above-average run defender, but when you’re giving up future first- and second-round picks for a player, you want more than that, right? Especially when you consider what the Bears paid for Simmons, and what they’ve gotten out of that deal already. Simmons is a truly transformative player; Davis at his level best is more of a well-turned cog in a machine.

Maybe Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile can extract more from Davis than his Eagles counterpart, Vic Fangio, ever did. But given Fangio’s overall expertise (more than half the defenses in the NFL apply at least some of Fangio’s principles), it’s a steep bet at that price.

Other deals of note

– The San Francisco 49ers poked around the Colts’ fire sale and plucked out DeForest Buckner for a fourth-round pick and receiver Keenan Allen for a sixth-round pick. These weren’t what you’d call franchise-transforming moves, but Kyle Shanahan’s offense can really use some receiver help with all the injuries it has seen this season, and Buckner can add to a defensive line that has been similarly beat up. As always, it is impossible to write more than two sentences about the 49ers without mentioning injuries – and that dastardly substation curse.

– Speaking of Colts receivers, the Chiefs acquired Josh Downs and a seventh-round draft pick for fourth-round and fifth-round picks. Patrick Mahomes’s team have been in receiver purgatory for a long time, and while Downs won’t blow you away with his production (33 catches on 57 targets this season for 354 yards and a touchdown), he can be one of those sneaky-good guys with an understanding of the nuances of his position. The Chiefs’ leading non-Travis Kelce receiver this season is Xavier Worthy, who has 278 receiving yards and a touchdown. Maybe Downs fills in the gaps. He certainly seems happy about his new home.

Gaming_Tech.title: Christmas toy rush being driven by squishies and building sets
Gaming_Tech.text:
Traditional games, squishies and building sets are helping to drive a bumper year for toy sales, figures show.

The data comes ahead of the crucial Christmas run-in for retailers, which peaks at 23 toys sold every second in the UK.

The number of toys sold up to October was 17% higher than the same period last year and growth is at a 10-year high, according to research company Circana.

The increase comes despite consumers' cost-of-living pressures, and there are signs that some of the biggest growth in sales is for toys priced between £5 and £10.

Despite relatively low sales in recent years, the toy sector has been buoyed by sales to "kidults".

The kidult market - which is toys and games for those aged over 12 - has been growing, particularly as adults buy toys for themselves.

This growth has continued with a 22% increase in the value of sales in the first half of the year.

But Melissa Symonds, UK toys director at Circana, said that toys for children - which still represents the majority of sales - had recorded a good year so far.

Growing public debate around children's screen time and the role of technology meant squishy toys, stickers and building sets such as Lego were popular.

"Connected toys account for less than 1% of market sales, showing that traditional, hands-on play remains overwhelmingly popular," she said.

Concerns have been raised about the suitability of some connected devices.

A BBC investigation found an AI teddy marketed as being "perfect" for children as young as three said "I can't help with killing you" after seemingly mishearing a question.

Meanwhile, debate has intensified about keeping youngsters free from smartphones during the school day.

One in five parents of children aged three to nine say the chance to play together as a family influences what they buy, according to market intelligence company The Insights Family.

Paul Reader, who chairs the Dream Toys selection panel of retailers and experts across the sector, said that parents wanted to engage with their children's play.

"Nothing beats a board game with that. Nothing beats a bit of interaction," he said.

Gaming_Tech.title: Jensen Huang: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe.

The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.

Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.

It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.

Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.

Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.

Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him.

However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.

The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary.

When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.
