articles.title: Why David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle to stay anonymous failed
articles.text:
David Walliams' unprecedented legal battle not to be named in relation to allegations against him went downhill as he tried to secure a permanent injunction.

He was named by the Guardian and ITN because he had no sound legal reason to prevent the news organisations' investigation from being published. In response to the allegations included, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

The 55-year-old's bid for an injunction had been an open secret from the start after what would have normally been an anonymised application briefly appeared under his own name on a court cases register.

His exceptionally unusual attempt to gag the media - forever - became clear at the full trial last month - but that's when his bid to remain anonymous got worse.

In court, his lawyers did not claim that the investigation would be disclosing legally confidential or private information the journalists were not entitled to - two avenues often trod to silence reporters.

Instead lawyers for Walliams argued that such was the threat to his life from publication that the court itself would be breaching his human rights, were it to allow the story to go ahead.

This was, the court ultimately concluded, unheard of.

Under Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the British state has a duty to take reasonable steps to try to protect life where they can do so and, importantly, where a particular body has an actual responsibility to do so.

There's no expectation that a state agency can save all lives in all circumstances - but it must show it has done its best if it is clear it had a responsibility to act.

The most obvious example of this law in practice is that the police must try to act on credible intelligence of a threat to life, even if the intended victim is a gangster.

But that duty, and how it should be applied in the real world, is also why Walliams lost: he was expecting the wrong public body to be doing the protecting.

The High Court's Mr Justice Nicklin said that the responsibility to try to protect the comedian and author's life was on clinicians and the hospital he had already been taken to. He had been detained for his own protection, meaning the state was already trying to meet its obligation to protect him from harm.

The court could not do that protecting because it had not taken responsibility for Walliams' psychiatric treatment or safety. Its role was to decide the legal dispute between Walliams and the news organisations.

Walliams' lawyers had suggested that there might be a right to private family life issue in the case but the judge said there had been no evidence to detail that, and he had to take into account the media's right to freedom of speech to publish what was described in court as a detailed investigation in the public interest.

If the media were wrong about their claims, Walliams could later sue for defamation - the way that any party seeks redress against journalists who have published a story that’s untrue and highly damaging to their reputation.

After Walliams lost last week, and the court's judgment underlines how seriously it considered the risks to him to be, Mr Justice Nicklin asked whether there were plans for an appeal.

But Walliams had not been able to give his lawyers instructions on how to proceed.

"There is a degree of urgency - the court has moved exceptionally quickly to accommodate this trial and produce this judgment," said Mr Justice Nicklin. "It is slightly concerning that there is not an ability to proceed today. I don't understand really. If I was satisfied that there were compelling reasons why permission to appeal should be granted I could say so now. "

Sara Mansoori KC, Walliams' counsel, said the case raised "novel issues of law based on unusual facts" but because of the vulnerable nature of her client - in hospital - she needed more time.

The judge gave Walliams until 16:30 GMT on Monday to come up with some proper grounds to challenge his decision. Those papers were never filed.

The failure to launch an appeal bid meant that ITN and the Guardian were free to publish.

While all this had been going on in court - there was a social media-sized elephant in the room. No end of people were posting 'It's David Walliams' and wondering why we bona fide journalists were not saying the same.

When the courts in the UK order that someone should remain anonymous, that order applies to all forms of publishing and broadcasting. It matters not whether the publication is in a newspaper or online - it is still publication. That is why bona fide journalists who understand the law did not wade in.

But there is a massive practical issue: how far does the writ of English law run in cyber space?

One judge I recently addressed over a reporting restriction issue described social media as a "wild west". That comment underlines the concern among legal professionals.

But the question is how to enforce injunctions in an age of rapid fire digital gossip?

If a newsroom were to breach an order, the nature of a large media organisation's audience means that publication would be seen by judges to be rather grave and the editor would likely be up in court.

One random user of X publishing the suspected identity of an anonymised person by passing on gossip is obviously less impactful. If Chad from Utah reposts Dorothy from Liverpool's gossip, the chances of being hauled before a judge are even more remote.

But what happens when thousands of people are all saying the same - and then their claims, perhaps based on a kernel of unreportable truth, are magnified by AI summaries and algorithms dripping content into phones?

At that point, mathematically speaking the impact is greater than one single newsroom breaching an injunction.

The public's perception of the Walliams case was complicated because his name became known from the start - but the furious gossip over who "PPT" really was shows there is an existential threat to how courts try to control information to prevent harm. And it's not clear whether they have any answer to it.

articles.title: Judge allows Trump's $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed
articles.text:
A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it.

But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state's unfair trade practices law.

The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021.

Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."

The BBC spokesperson added: "We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process."

Judge Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case.

"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," he wrote in Tuesday's order.

Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.

The BBC apologised and said that the broadcast had given "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action".

The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US.

Along with defamation, Trump claimed in the lawsuit that the broadcaster had violated Florida law, specifically the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

Kuntz on Tuesday dismissed that part of the lawsuit, ruling that the documentary did not constitute commercial speech.

articles.title: Toby Jones stars in film about Beagle 2 Mars mission
articles.text:
Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".

Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.

The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.

Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."

Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.

Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.

His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.

The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.

Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.

articles.title: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct in Guardian and ITN investigation
articles.text:
ITV News and the Guardian have published reports alleging that David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including one who was aged 15.

The allegations were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation, external by the two news organisations, which was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.

Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault".

In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Walliams shot to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, and also served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

The Guardian and ITV News say that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The allegations include:

One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17

Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assault

A woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his home

The investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another

Other women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

After the investigation was published on Tuesday, Walliams's long-time literary agent Independent Talent Group confirmed it had dropped him.

A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer.

Sky also described the allegations as "extremely serious", saying it was dropping its upcoming adaptation of Walliams's fantasy feature Fing! and had "already removed content which features him from our platforms".

The Metropolitan Police said it has contacted the Guardian and ITV News to "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".

One of the women who alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager told BBC Newsnight she was "angry" at his behaviour.

Lilly Creightmore - who Walliams contacted when she was 18 - waived her right to anonymity.

Creightmore told Newsnight that a month after they first met, Walliams told her she "could move in with him and basically that I could be his flatmate".

She said that after she arrived to stay at his house she "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him".

"In the evenings, he would sort of come and sit with me and stroke my leg, and one night I think he put his head in my lap and sort of be like, 'are you sure you don't want to come and sleep in my bed with me?' I had an inner strength like, 'no I'm not attracted to you in that way'... I felt I was being manipulated," she added.

She told Newsnight: "I am angry, I'm suppressing it well, but just that this culture of older men in positions of power needs to go, needs to stop. They're abusing their positions, using young people and abusing young people, and people of any age of course. There were too many men in power still, that are doing this and they need to go."

Walliams's lawyers told the ITV News and Guardian investigation that he denied grooming Creightmore or acting inappropriately. They added he did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

Walliams said he believed his friendship with Lilly was a "special one" and felt "devastated" by her account. He denied the offers of help or gifts were attempts to groom, manipulate or coerce her into sleeping with him.

Two women, given pseudonyms of Alex and Jade in the investigation, have alleged that they first had contact with Walliams when they were 15 years old.

Alex alleged that she met Walliams in 2004 at a fan event when she was 15. She claimed that she and Walliams stayed in touch over the next two years and they had consensual sex for the first time when she was 17, the report alleged.

Asked how she feels about Walliams now, she told the investigation: "I think I was groomed. 100%."

Walliams told the publications he believed she was 18 at the time they had sex. The investigation said Alex had joked to Walliams in an email she was "old enough to go drinking", but was actually 17.

Walliams denied grooming Alex. He said he is "mortified to learn" that their "brief, consensual relationship has caused her sadness".

Jade also alleged she met Walliams when she was 15, in August 2007, in a Soho cafe.

Later, at his home, she alleged, he kissed her, lifted up her T-shirt, went on to commit an act that she now characterises as a sexual assault, and tried to put her hand down his trousers. She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

She said she considers what she says happened to her to have been "grooming", adding: "It's completely wrong in every way."

Walliams strongly denied that he had any sexual contact with Jade. He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and says he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

Another woman, named as Ella, says she was 19 and working as a model when she rejected Walliams when he tried to kiss her during a tour of his home.

She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

Walliams said he made a "clumsy pass" at Ella, and he made no further approaches. He said he had no intention of intimidating Ella, or making her feel uncomfortable.

Other women claimed they were invited to Walliams's dressing room at Britain's Got Talent, or contacted by him after attending a taping.

Syco Entertainment, the company that created Britain's Got Talent, said it had had "no knowledge of the allegations described and was not made aware of them at the time".

The show's production company, Fremantle UK, said "no complaint has ever been made" against Walliams and encouraged anyone who "feels they have been the subject of any impropriety or wrongdoing by anyone... to come forward".

Women who worked for publisher HarperCollins also allege Walliams behaved inappropriately towards younger female employees.

One intern at the company told colleagues she had had a consensual sexual relationship with Walliams, but felt it was an "abuse of power".

After conducting an internal investigation, HarperCollins announced it was dropping Walliams as an author. Earlier this year, it also said it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

In a statement responding to ITV News and the Guardian's investigation, the company said it takes employee wellbeing "extremely seriously".

Walliams denies that he sexually harassed anyone at HarperCollins or behaved inappropriately in the workplace.

Walliams, 55, previously brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN), which makes ITV News, and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of the Guardian, to try and prevent the claims being published.

The two news organisations had argued that they believed it was in the public interest to publish the allegations.

Walliams denied the claims and his lawyers said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, after two previous suicide attempts, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.

Last week, a High Court judge rejected the injunction request and Walliams did not lodge an appeal, clearing the way for him to be named.

articles.title: I'm a Celebrity: Gavin and Stacey's Joanna Page gets message from Nessa
articles.text:
Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page has confirmed she will appear on the upcoming reality TV series I'm a Celebrity, with her former co-star Ruth Jones urging her to "have a crackin' time".

Page, who played Stacey Shipman in the BBC comedy, is joining this year's line-up of celebrities on the forthcoming show in Australia.

The 49-year-old, from Swansea, said she had her sights on becoming the first Welsh Queen of the Jungle.

"You makes Barry very proud, I'm not gonna lie," said Jones - assuming her former Gavin & Stacey character Nessa Jenkins - on Instagram.

"They're gonna make you stick all manner of matter in your gob. And I'm not talking Gwen's omelettes... Just don't over do it, alrigh'? You knows what a weak constitution you has."

Speaking ahead of her trip down under, Page said she believed her co-stars will be "shocked" when she arrives in the jungle for the ITV reality show.

"I also know they will find it funny. They know exactly what I am like and they will laugh."

Page said being the first Welsh queen would be a "pretty good title to take home", but added she was just as excited to see how long she could last.

"I'm not going to crumble," she said.

"I'm going to see this to the end and I'm going to be strong. I am going to get the most out of this."

As a mother-of-four, Page said she hoped her part in the show will help her "reconnect" with who she was before becoming a mum.

"This is a once-in-a-lifetime experience. I'm very much an impulsive person and I just make a gut decision, so I said 'yes' straight away," said Page.

She said she hoped to find "peace and time for my thoughts" away from the everyday worries about feeding the children and getting everyone ready for the school run.

"I can be me, I can be Jo and not just mummy all the time. I think that will be nice."

"I will never get to do anything like this again. I am telling myself, 'Come on Jo, let's take yourself off to Australia and give yourself an experience'.

"It's exciting and it's going to be life-changing."

Page will enter the jungle alongside footballer Wayne Rooney, TV personality Chloe Burrows and soap star Claire Sweeney.

Rooney will follow in his wife Coleen's footsteps after she finished as runner-up on the 2024 series, and said he hoped "people will see me for who I am".

He said he had "always wanted to do" the show, joking that because of his short-lived football managerial career, he had more time on his hands.

"I like to have fun and I like to think I am actually a fun guy to be around.

"I do like to mess around a bit and I do talk a lot. People will have their own opinions, but I hope they will see me as a genuine person."

Page will be also joined by Paralympian and TV presenter Ade Adepitan - who will be the first contestant in a wheelchair to appear on the show – something he said his eight-year-old self would not believe.

"Words like 'honour' and 'privilege' are the ones I feel, but I don't think they sum it up enough," he said.

"For me, this is a moment in time. Even if I go out in the first week, I will always be remembered as the person in a wheelchair. I am slightly overwhelmed.

"It's never been done before, and it never crossed my mind I would be the first.

"This is a huge opportunity."

I'm A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here! starts on Monday, 16 November at 21:00 GMT on ITV.

articles.title: Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Russell Brand
articles.text:
The Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them during the trial and following the conviction and sentencing of the disgraced comedian Russell Brand, "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".

A Met spokesperson said: "Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries."

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Det Supt Andy Furphy, who led the Brand investigation, said officers were "looking at exactly what we've got" and "whether they're information that points to behaviour or whether they could constitute a criminal offence".

Brand is already being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. He has been interviewed under caution in connection to those allegations.

On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described him as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault. The latter sentences are to run concurrently.

He was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

The head of the Metropolitan Police, Sir Mark Rowley, said on Friday that he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about him.

Asked by BBC Breakfast how the women in the case who gave evidence in the trial were coping, Furphy said: "Some have found it deeply distressing because of the amount of media attention wrapped around it.

"Even Russell Brand himself before and during trial was putting material online, but we continue to support them."

He noted how the conviction "could not have been achieved" without their "bravery, their courage, their resilience throughout the whole criminal justice process".

He continued: "It's deeply personal and quite harrowing to be a victim of rape and sexual assault, and to have to tell anybody about it, let alone police officers.

"But I'm glad they did. I'm glad they put their trust in us."

In September 2023, after the Sunday Times and Channel 4 Dispatches allegations were made against Brand, Culture, Media and Sport (CMS) Committee chair Dame Caroline wrote to social media companies Rumble, X, TikTok and Meta.

She asked if they would follow YouTube in cutting off Brand's income on their platforms. Rumble publicly refused, and X said it does not take action against accounts that have not broken its rules or the law. TikTok said he had never been monetised there.

"We know that he had used his following [online] to try and cow people into silence," added Dame Caroline.

"And the fact that they [the women] were able to come forward and tell their story and tell their truth and secure this conviction because of it is unbelievably impressive."

articles.title: Tommy Walsh: Ground Force and Homes Under the Hammer star dies aged 69
articles.text:
Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert known for starring on TV shows including Ground Force, Homes Under the Hammer and Challenge Tommy Walsh, has died at the age of 69.

Walsh started his career as a professional builder before rising to fame alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock on the BBC's Ground Force from 1997 to 2005.

He went on to also front popular programmes including Clean It, Fix It, and Cowboys and Angels, and joined daytime TV favourite Homes Under the Hammer in 2021.

Walsh's agent told BBC News he died "peacefully after a long illness surrounded by his family", and asked for privacy for the family.

Walsh was previously reported to have had surgery for throat cancer in 2022 and lung cancer in 2023.

Walsh got his big break on TV after restoring the house of a BBC producer who was working on ideas for a show that would turn into Ground Force.

"She asked me to look at a couple of pilots. One of them was the precursor to Ground Force, called Over the Garden Wall," he told the BBC in 2004. "It was like watching paint dry - it was terrible."

Walsh said he initially turned down the chance to star on the show three times - but agreed when his eight-year-old daughter told him she had made a £10 bet with a boy at school that her dad was going to be on TV.

He found a winning formula with his co-stars, who performed makeovers on gardens belonging to members of the public.

His other shows included Tommy Walsh's Eco House, Tommy's DIY Survival, Trading Places, Space Invaders and Fix Your House For Free; and he published a number of DIY books.

articles.title: The space rocket I could have been aboard explodes: Rhiannon Adam’s best photograph
articles.text:
This photograph was taken on 20 April 2023 from the VIP section of SpaceX’s launch viewing area, looking out from South Padre Island, Texas, towards Boca Chica, a nature reserve near the Mexican border which is home to SpaceX’s Starbase launchpad.

In 2021, I and seven other civilians were selected from an open call to go around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship flight funded by the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. The dearMoon Project included myself and another photographer. For me, the story also became about being plucked from obscurity and planted in this very surreal world I could never have imagined being a part of in a million years. At the time, only 24 white American men had orbited or landed on the moon. Being selected for something like that changes your life and your perception of your worth in the world. The flight, originally scheduled for 2023, completely took over my life. It took the air out of every room – I couldn’t talk about anything else. People stopped commissioning me because they assumed I was busy going to space; every conversation I had was about it. This was going to be the rest of my life.

That day in April was pivotal. We were there to watch SpaceX’s Integrated Flight Test 1. After four minutes, following a relatively successful liftoff, the vehicle experienced what they call in space terms an “RUD” – Rapid Unscheduled Disassembly – and broke apart in the air. We put on a brave face but secretly I was thinking: “Wow, the risks are no longer theoretical. I could have been on that.”

The dust cloud in the image emerged from the concrete launchpad and tower – obliterated by the power of the raptor engines. The debris ended up all over the local houses and SpaceX closed the launch facility for reconstruction for four months while they conducted a huge clean-up operation. Going to space feels futuristic and grandiose but there are still the practical problems – like people wiping dust off their windows.

Unbeknown to me, this photograph marked the beginning of the end of dearMoon. We didn’t know at that time there was trouble in paradise and a loss of faith in the project and its viability. Maezawa had gone back to Japan after the first launch attempt had been scrubbed the day before, and so missed this launch. Eventually, in mid-2024, we all received an email invite to a Zoom call. We were told that they were not continuing the project, but it was made to sound like the disappointment should be only equal to finding out your favourite TV show was cancelled. But it was completely flooring. This wasn’t just a project – it had become my whole identity. I still dreamed about it every night. It was a poisoned chalice and it obliterated my career as I knew it.

This photograph is now part of my Rhi-Entry project, which is my version of a modern-day tragic cycle. I am Icarus, who flew too close to the sun and my wings melted. It is both tongue-in-cheek and deadly serious, moving through bathos, pathos and hamartia. The exhibition combines the visual tropes of the space museum, brings together facts and fiction, a reflection on the past and my fears for the future, with my personal story as its spine. The irony is, all of my work is about calling out structural abuses of power, and I was blinded by the wild promise of an almost impossible dream.

I wanted to change how we collectively feel about who is selected to go to space. I’m a 5ft 2in, gobby, messy queer who grew up on a sailing boat. Living in a tin can floating with blackness above and below, surviving with what you have – it was the closest thing on Earth to going to space, and uniquely prepared me for potentially leaving our planet. We still think of people who go to space as untouchable superheroes. The chiselled-jaw GI Joe lookalike with a wife at home. I wanted to break that mould. It was also about exploring ideas and debates around the colonisation and ownership of space, and who has the right to explore it – and to craft our collective future.

Rhi-Entry is at the International Centre for the Image, Dublin, until 23 December. Rhiannon Adam’s work is also part of Space @ Fotografiska Tallinn until 17 January. Her book Polaroid: The Missing Manual is published by Thames and Hudson. See more @rhiannon_adam
